## Good architecture

Goal of architecture is to reduce work on creation and maintenance of the system.

Identify the load-bearing assumption behind the proposed shape; ask yourself - what is the cheapest real example that could prove this design assumption wrong? 

Check it when practical, preferably against external reality rather than our own documents and tests.

If falsified, realign.
If unverified and load-bearing, preserve the uncertainty explicitly.

## Domain awareness

During codebase exploration, also look for existing documentation:

### File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── docs/
│   ├── adr/
│   │   ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│   │   └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
│   ├── architecture.md
│   └── glossary.md
└── src/
```

Create files lazily — only when you have something to write. If no `docs/glossary.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.
</straw-dog>

## During the session

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0001.0001">
### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `docs/glossary.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y — which is it?"

This cuts both ways: before *you* propose a name, check the glossary yourself — including its _Avoid_ lists, which are reservations, not suggestions. If every synonym for a concept is avoided, that is a designed constraint telling you which word the project has chosen; work within it rather than proposing around it.
</straw-dog>

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">
### Check whether it was already decided

Before treating a question as open, search the ADRs and architecture docs for it. A surprising amount of "open" questions are accepted decisions the code drifted from — the answer then is "implement the ADR", not a fresh trade-off analysis. Cite the deciding document when you find one.
</straw-dog>

**The work.** 01-0010.0220 lets a project's settings decide which of the method's rules its tree
carries. A setting changed through the agent's call runs the installer at once. This question is
the other path: the person edits the local file by hand — the dial is theirs, and today every
setting is set that way — and starts a session. Until the installer runs, the tree's installed
blocks say one thing and its settings another.

**Necessity gate.** Customer: the person of any recipient tree, this one included. Problem: a
tree whose entry file still shows debugging after its person switched it off, or shows the dial at
yesterday's rung. Why the existing behaviour cannot satisfy it: nothing runs the installer but
being asked, `harness.py <target> --update`; `/maintain` would find the mismatch as drift, at its
own pace. The need holds while settings are edited by hand at all.

**Facts that bear.** The session-start hook (`hook.sh` → `questions.py --hook <host>`) already
writes the tree at session start — the store's session rows — and by the hosts edge's invariant
exits clean whatever happens, a problem becoming a line of context; it has never written an
instruction file. The installer refuses what it cannot satisfy and reports it (`harness.py`,
*refuse what cannot be satisfied*), which wants a reader. A session whose entry file moved under
it is told and reads it again (01-0018.0010, Ready). Two sessions may start in one tree within a
minute (the sessions list).

**The shared assumption of the fork below**: that a setting is changed by hand at all. The
alternative dissolves it: the call is the one way — the person runs it too, in a shell, since the
host refuses only an agent's call on a person-only setting — and a hand edit is drift for
`/maintain`. Put first.

**Fork — who runs the installer after a hand edit, and when:**

- **A. The hook runs it at session start.** Always matching, no step. Against: a hook writing
  instruction files silently, before any agent exists; its refusals have no reader and must
  still exit clean, so a half-applied tree goes unsaid; two starting sessions race on the same
  files; whether the host reads the entry file before or after its start hook is unverified.

  settings moved; the session runs the installer before its first reply, below the dial, says
  so in one line, and the change lands in its first commit; the installer's refusals reach a
  reader; the hosts edge keeps its invariant — the hook reports, never repairs. Against: a host
  without a start hook leaves it to `/recall`'s own check.

  says so. Against: the person already acted by editing; a second step is weight the work does
  not need, and the tree reads wrong until it is taken.

Decisive fact for B over A: the installer refuses and reports, and a hook has no one to report
to; for B over C: the hand edit was the ask.

**О чём работа.** Тикет [01-0010.0220](docs/tickets/01-0010.0220-a-tree-carries-the-methods-text-its-settings-call-for.md) даёт настройкам проекта решать, какие правила метода несёт его дерево. Если настройку меняет агент своим вызовом, инсталлятор запускается тут же. Этот вопрос — о другом пути: человек правит локальный файл руками — ручка его, и сегодня все настройки ставятся так — и открывает сессию. Пока инсталлятор не прогнан, блоки в дереве говорят одно, настройки другое.

**Нужно ли это вообще.** Заказчик — человек любого дерева-получателя, нашего тоже. Проблема — файл входа всё ещё показывает отладку после того, как человек её выключил, или ручку на вчерашней ступени. Почему нынешнее поведение не спасает: инсталлятор запускается только по просьбе, а /maintain нашёл бы расхождение как дрейф, в свой срок. Нужда держится ровно до тех пор, пока настройки вообще правят руками.

**И это первый вопрос — общая посылка развилки.** Обе ветви предполагают, что ручная правка настроек остаётся. Альтернатива растворяет развилку: единственный способ сменить настройку — вызов, и человек тоже им пользуется, из шелла; хост отказывает лишь агенту на настройках «только человек». nothing about being load-bearing — an implementation method is a shape too. → [glossary](.agents/glossary.md).

- **The shape's context.** Explore shape context - what is the shape one of? what are its relationships? does its scope overlap any other shape? Look in this tree and in every tree core reaches.
- **The shape's structure.** Explore shape structure - how this shape is/can be built? does expanding its structure change the contract or even what the shape is?

## Document load-bearing, code&comment the rest

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">
A project's architecture, ADRs and glossary are the home for:
- Constitution — identity semantics, consistency model, source-of-truth rules
- Structure — service boundaries, data ownership, event/data flows, extension seams
- Load-bearing — see the definition below

A decision forms in the body of the question it answers and lands in one of these as it is made —
as a straw dog while an open question's answer can still change it. A decision about a
mechanism lands in that mechanism's doc, and what was refuted in its evidence.
</straw-dog>

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">
Bad architectural documentation:
- Forecasts are stored in MongoDB collection forecast_hourly.

Better:
- Historical forecast issues must remain independently addressable by (location, valid_time, issue_time) because validation compares what was known at different issue times.
</straw-dog>

## What makes a thing "load-bearing"

- A decision or invariant whose violation would cause multiple parts of the system to become wrong, not merely require local refactoring.
- A thing is load-bearing when several of these are true: has high blast radius, crosses boundaries (i.e. services, persistence, APIs, ownership), other decisions depend on it, it protects an invariant,
is expensive to reverse, holds non-obvious rationale, long-standing.

- Counter-test: if it can be changed locally without understanding the rest of the architecture, it is not load-bearing.

## The loop

Two rings, joined at /align.

    session:   wake with /recall → /align → /conclude → (next session)
    delivery:  /ticket → /plan → /implement → /verify → /maintain → /ticket

/align opens the delivery ring and is where it returns whenever a decision is needed:
<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">a load-bearing shape is aligned on its question until its `Where it stands` is accepted,</straw-dog> /plan when the governing docs contradict, /verify when a finding needs one, /maintain when maintenance surfaces one. /ticket⇄/plan and /implement⇄/verify iterate as pairs.

Human checkpoints: every decision at /align; a question's `Where it stands` accepted; and
whatever stands at or above its ladder's dial under [Autonomy](#autonomy).

Do not reopen an accepted decision without new evidence.

### Helpers

- /impact determines the scope and load-bearingness of the shape. Use it to evaluate work volume and its ticketing shape (<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">an align on its question for load-bearing work, tickets for mechanical</straw-dog>), work units slicing or whether a shape deserves further investigation due to hidden complexity.
- /discover to investigate hidden complexity, by detecting what else the shape is.

## Self-improvement

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0012">
- A rule that was in place and did not fire was usually worded wrong. Register the failure in docs/rule-failures.md, or strike the entry it repeats, and propose the amendment that would have made it fire; /mechanism and /skill-up hold the means. Land the amendment in the same pass, showing its text first.
- A slip no rule covers is registered there too, described broadly enough to recognise its repeat;
  one proposes no rule.
- Keeping the register: an entry names the rules that were in play and proposes the amendment; a repeat strikes the entry it repeats rather than opening a second; an entry closes when its amendment lands, or is refused with its reason. Nothing here authorises deleting a rule.
</straw-dog>

## Autonomy

Autonomy is a dial on a ladder. A method whose decisions differ in how far their consequences
reach has a ladder, its rungs ordered by that reach and declared by the method's mechanism; a
method without one states which of its decisions are the agent's and which the person's. A
decision's rung is read from what it decides, never from the record that holds it; a case between
two rungs takes the higher.

- 🤖 Below the dial the agent settles and acts on its own.
- ✋ At the dial it settles, and shows the person before acting.
- 💬 Above it, it settles nothing: it brings the options and a recommendation, and the person
  decides.

A question carries its highest rung on each ladder it touches and stops for the person while that
rung is at or above the ladder's dial. Mending a violation is the work of the rung the mended thing
is on. Work closes with its commit once `/verify` passes on it; a push follows the project's way of
working with git, as its local file states.

The project sets each dial in its local block; an unset dial is at the lowest rung. The agent never
writes its dial<straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0005">, and the host refuses an edit that changes it</straw-dog>.

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">
Development's ladder, lowest first:

| rung | a decision on it — as the person is shown it |
|---|---|
| code | writing the code inside agreed work |
| a feature | what one piece of work should deliver |
| load-bearing | a load-bearing architectural decision, e.g. module boundaries |
| a product slice | what gets built next |
| the whole product | what the project is for |

An install proposes the dial at *a feature*.
</straw-dog>

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0012.0001">
Self-improvement's ladder, lowest first:

| rung | a decision on it — as the person is shown it |
|---|---|
| a wording | rewording an instruction, its meaning unchanged |
| a script | fixing a script that carries an instruction out |
| a rule | changing an instruction or a skill |
| the method | changing the way of working |

An install proposes the dial at *a rule*.
</straw-dog>

## Project-local

<installed by="mechanism-shape">
**R7** A project's own answers and overrides are authored in one file beside the entry file,
`local.rules.md`, in the rules-file format, and reach a file only as the local block — the
installed block whose owner is `local` — which the installer writes after every mechanism's block
there, so the project's answer is what a reader meets after core's rule. An override names the rule it
overrides. A local change to a rule is written in the local file, never into a skill or the entry
file, and re-installed. The local block is the project's,
not core's, and a redeploy preserves it.
</installed>

<installed by="local">
**L1** This repository develops the shared dev harness using its own loop; its own architecture and
progress live in docs/ like any other project's — the instance half doing its job, not a leak.
Terms: docs/glossary.md, this project's own; the method's are .agents/glossary.md's. What each
version of the entry contract changed: docs/research/entry-contract-findings.md.

**L2** development=a feature · self-improvement=a rule. Push each commit as it lands.

**L4** debug=on

**L5** Run a Python script with `uv run --offline --no-project python <script>`.

**L7** A correction that lands as a rule in this tree is not also written to the host's own memory
store outside the repository — Claude Code's auto-memory directory and its kin; that store holds
only what no record in this tree carries.

**L9** Write a reply's prose the way Lem wrote: plain, exact and dry, an argument the reader can follow,
irony where it is earned. It is never agent-speak, the voice of a tool narrating its own steps, and
it invents nothing: what it tells is what happened. Tables, decisions and text proposed for a
record keep the exactness their forms ask.

**L12** At most 8 open questions are in work at once — a running session standing on one or under it, or
its owner ticket In progress. The ninth is opened and placed, and waits until one leaves work.
</installed>

## Straw dogs

Wrap anything an open question's answer will change, as you write it — or, for text already
written, in the pass that opens the question: `<straw-dog question="q-N">`, bound to the question
whose answer will rewrite it, or in code a `TODO` naming `q-N` first. Treat *not yet*, *until*,
*once it exists*, *for now*, *untested* in your own text as the same signal: find the question, or
open one. Wrap at the authored home, never where the harness installs or derives it. Write the body
to stand on its own: it is what a recipient receives once the wrapper is stripped, so it names no
question or ticket — the binding does. Leave what no open question would change unwrapped.

Follow a straw dog like any other rule until it is due, as the listing and the wake report; then
act on reality, rewrite it to what is now true, and do not treat the contradiction as a violation.

## The rules file

```md
# <slug> — rules installed into skills

| target | anchor |
|---|---|
| `.agents/skills/maintain/SKILL.md` | `## Installed from other mechanisms` |

## R1 — <title>

- **target** `.agents/skills/maintain/SKILL.md`
- **authority** the user, 2026-09-07

<rule>
Check a record-bearing mechanism's records with its maintainer script — format never
content, live rows only. Where the script is missing, write it: that is the maintenance.
</rule>
```

Prose before the table is the file's own preamble and is not read.

- **The anchor table** names every target the file installs into, one row each: the target a
  backticked repo-relative path, the anchor a backticked line that occurs exactly once in the
  target, whole and newline-terminated. **A mechanism has one place in a target**: a target
  named twice is refused.
- **One `## ` section per rule.** The heading's first token, before ` — `, is the rule's id,
  unique in the file. **target** repeats, one path per bullet, each a row of the table.
  **authority** is who decided the rule and when, read and reported, never interpreted.
  **overrides**, at most once, names the core rule this one replaces as `` `<slug>/<id>` ``: the
  slug must have a rules file, the id must be in it, and that rule must name every target this
  section names — read from its declared targets, never from whether its block is present — or
  the section is refused naming this rule. The citation is rendered into the block, after the
  id, as `*(overrides <slug>/<id>)*`, so a reader meets the disagreement where they meet the rule.
- **The body** is the span between a line that is exactly `<rule>` and a line that is exactly
  `</rule>`, installed byte for byte. It holds no markdown citation — the mover rewrites a
  relative link per the file it sits in, so one body in two directories would drift apart — no
  heading line, no `<installed` or `</installed>`, and no `<straw-dog>`. A section with two spans,
  or none, is refused.
- **A rule that expires is wrapped around its section**: the tag opens before the heading and
  closes after `</rule>`, outside the body, so a target receives the rule and never the wrapper.
  A tag inside a body is refused.

**What the installer writes**, per target: one block holding every rule of the file that names
it, in file order, each a paragraph opening with its id, into the section the anchor heads:

```md
<installed by="mechanism-shape">
**R1** Check a record-bearing mechanism's records with its maintainer script — format never
content, live rows only. Where the script is missing, write it: that is the maintenance.

**R2** Compare a mechanism against what governs it with line endings normalised, its evidence
excluded, and installed blocks excluded.
</installed>
```

The block is found by its tag, never by its body, and compared whole against what the rules
file renders. **A rules file's block is installed in every target it names, or the check
fails**: an absent block, a drifted one, and a block nothing owns — its slug has no rules file,
or that file does not name the file the block sits in — are each a diagnostic. Every example of the tag or an anchor in a doc sits in a code span or fence, on one
line; the installer looks through code and never takes an example for the thing.

The installer: `inject_rules.py <slug> --install [--overwrite]`, `<slug> --retract`, `--check`.
A named mode or a refusal; every target validated before anything is written; retraction
leaves the target byte-identical; a differing block refuses until the caller says overwrite,
and then the block is replaced whole and the report carries what it replaced. The contract is
the architecture's; the entry file owns the prohibition on editing a block in place.

**The project's own rules file is one more source.** `local.rules.md` sits beside the entry
file, outside the core directory, in this same grammar, and is read as the slug `local` — a
mechanism directory of that name is refused. Its block must be the last in its file, so anchor a

# Edge record format

One record per edge, a living document at `docs/edge/<edge>.md`, named by the edge — `hosts.md`,
`installation.md`, `mcp.md`. No numbers, no `done/`: the record never completes, and its history
is git's. An edge things attach to keeps one sidecar per extension at
`docs/edge/<edge>/<extension>.md`.

An **edge** is where the system meets those who consume it or extend it. Its record holds what the
system promises them, what it requires of what attaches to it, the checks a new attachment passes,
where each attached thing stands, the edge's open questions, and its staged evolution. The
audience is the project at work, user and agents. Text written for a consumer or an extender — a
tool description, a public API doc, the front page, an install guide — is **derived from** the
record and stays a subset of it.

The record informs. Nothing an integration needs to work is read from it: the integration is code
and configuration in its own home, and the record names it.

## The record

```md
# Edge — {Name}

- **Status:** Stub | Normative | Normative (tentative)

## Contract

## Invariants

## Extending

## Extensions

## Concerns

## Roadmap
```

Sections appear in this order and no others. `Extending` and `Extensions` appear together, on an
edge things attach to, or neither does.

def _handed_off(source: Source, wanted: Ref, target: str, overwrite: bool) -> int:
    """An update run by the incoming ref's own installer, from that ref's core unpacked beside the
    clone: the tree's installer is as old as its last install and cannot know what a later ref
    brings, while the incoming one reads what an earlier one left. Pinned to the resolved commit,
    so both read one ref; its report is the run's."""
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="harness-incoming-") as scratch:
        incoming = Path(scratch)
        for path, data in source.files(wanted).items():
            (incoming / path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            (incoming / path).write_bytes(data)
        script = incoming / SCRIPTS / "harness.py"
        if not script.is_file():
            raise Refused(f"update: {wanted.announced} holds no {SCRIPTS}harness.py to run the update")
        arguments = [target, "--update", "--from", source.repository, "--at", wanted.commit]
        handed = subprocess.run(
            [sys.executable, str(script), *arguments, *(["--overwrite"] if overwrite else [])],
            capture_output=True, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace",
            env={**os.environ, HANDED_OFF: "the tree's installer"},

    print(handed.stdout, end="")
    print(handed.stderr, end="", file=sys.stderr)

- **Extending** — the checks a new extension passes, in general terms: a numbered list, one check

# A tree carries only the method's text its settings call for — implementation plan

- **record of** what it intends to become

**Authored:** 2026-10-23

Implements [01-0010.0220](../tickets/01-0010.0220-a-tree-carries-the-methods-text-its-settings-call-for.md):
a mechanism declares its settings, a rule names the condition of its installation, the project
sets values in its local file, and the installer writes a rule into its targets only while its
condition holds. The decisions are
[q-0037.0006.0026](../questions/q-0037.0006.0026-how-does-a-project-choose-which-of-the-methods-text-its-tree-carries.md)'s,
its forms under *Proposed forms* and the passes after.

## Governing boundaries

- **The rules file's grammar** is the format shelf's
  ([MECHANISM-FORMAT.md](../../.agents/skills/mechanism/MECHANISM-FORMAT.md), *The rules file*):
  the anchor table, one section per rule, `target`, `authority`, `overrides`, the body between
  `<rule>` edges. The declaration table, the `when` line and the local file's settings table land
  there, as grammar; nothing here invents a second home.
- **The installer's contract** is the architecture's
  ([Installed blocks](../architecture.md#installed-blocks)): a named mode or a refusal; every
  target validated before anything is written; retraction byte-identical; a differing block
  refused until the caller says overwrite, then replaced whole and reported. A conditioned rule
  is one more thing the renderer reads; the contract does not move.
- **R7**: the project's answers live in `local.rules.md` and reach a file only as the local block.
  The settings table is one more thing that file authors; its values reach a file only through
  the installer.
- **R4**: an index is rendered on request and never committed beside its records. The
  consolidated settings table is an index of the declarations and the local file.
- **The entry file's *Autonomy***: the project sets each dial in its local block, and the agent
  never writes its dial — the host refuses the edit (01-0010.0125's shape).
- **The hosts edge** ([hosts.md](../edge/hosts.md)): the hook never fails the host; a problem
  becomes a line of context.
- **A document informs**: the edge record names the renderer; nothing reads the record to work.
- **Decision 2 of q-0037.0009.0021**: debugging's text reaches a tree as installed blocks of its
  own mechanism, never one text read behind a switch. This ticket supplies the switch; the
  mechanism is 01-0016.0020's.

## Impact

**Impact.** `inject_rules.py`: the parser reads tables by their header, reads a declaration table
and `when` lines, resolves settings from the local file's table or the default, renders a target's
block from the rules whose conditions hold, treats a target left with no rule as one whose block
is removed, and gains a run over every source and a call that changes a setting. Its check: a
`when` naming an undeclared setting or value, a local value no declaration holds, a setting
declared twice, a block whose content disagrees with the settings. `harness.py`'s `_install_rules`
is that run, so the install and the update read settings for free. The format shelf: three
forms. `local.rules.md` of this tree: a settings table. `/harness`: two occasions in its
description, the table shown. `/maintain`: the injector's check already reaches it as M-rules;
a block disagreeing with its settings is one more diagnostic there, no new rule. The hosts
edge: a line at session start. Tests: `test_inject_rules.py` for every new form and refusal,
`test_harness.py` for the run.

**Hidden edges.** The anchor-table parser matches any row of two code spans, so a local settings
table of two code spans would be read as anchors: tables must be told by their header before
the first new row is written. A recipient updated before its local file has a table stands at
every default — safe, and the update's report says it. The dial's rows in the table are the
person's: the host's refusal of a dial edit must learn the table's row, or the table waits for
01-0010.0125. A run of the installer moves the entry file under running sessions
(01-0018.0010). Every mechanism's fingerprint moves at the format change. A setting's declaring
mechanism must exist before any rule can use it: `debug` has none until 01-0016.0020 builds
debugging, and the dials have none until the ladder mechanisms exist — the ticket's live
criteria have no declared setting to stand on (challenge 1).

**Leave alone.** The debug blocks' content and their move (01-0016.0020). Which method
(01-0017.0020). The host's refusal itself (01-0010.0125). The session-row writes of the hook.

**Recommendation.** Proceed as one slice, once the three challenges below are aligned: the
machinery is one contract; what is unsettled is which live setting proves it, where the wake's
line comes from, and what the edge record is.

## Challenges for `/align`

1. **No declared setting exists for the live criteria.** A `when` needs a declaring mechanism.
   `debug` is debugging's, unbuilt (01-0016.0020, *own align precedes*); the dials are the ladder
   mechanisms', undeclared (q-0037.0010.0002.0005, q-0037.0012.0001). The machinery can be proved
   whole on fixture trees — the suite already builds scratch repositories with rules files — but
   criteria 3 and 4 name this tree. Options: (a) the debugging mechanism's rules file lands with
   this ticket, holding the `debug` declaration and the rules now reading *Under debug=on* in
   other mechanisms' files gain `when debug=on` — 01-0016.0020 shrinks to the texts that leave
   the entry file and the scripts; (b) criterion 3 (the dial from the table) is deferred to the
   ladder mechanisms as a straw dog and the live proof is `debug` under (a); (c) the live
   criteria wait, the ticket proving itself on fixtures alone. Recommended: (a) with (b) —
   `debug` is the switch the whole question began with, and the dial has no declarer to wait for.
2. **The wake's line.** The decided flow has the wake report a tree whose blocks disagree with its
   settings. The wake is the questions mechanism's (`questions.py --hook` through `hook.sh`); the
   detector is the injector's check. Options: (a) `hook.sh` runs the injector's check after the
   wake and appends its one line in the host's form — `hook.sh` becomes a shared part, claimed
   by the always-on mechanism as every shared part is; (b) the questions mechanism calls the
   injector's check inside the wake — one mechanism's script reading another's, a *Relies on*
   row; (c) a second hook entry per host, owned by mechanism-shape, merged by the harness as
   core's hooks are — one more process at start and the host-form code twice. Recommended: (a).
3. **The edge record and R4.** The question decided *the installer's run writes the table as the
   edge record `docs/edge/settings.md`*. R4 forbids committing an index beside its records, and
   the edge format says a record informs and nothing reads it to work. Options: (a) the record is
   hand-written in the edge format — the contract, the invariants with their validators, and a
   pointer to the renderer `inject_rules.py --settings` — and the table is rendered on request,
   never committed; (b) the decision stands and R4 takes an exception. Recommended: (a); the
   question's decision is amended to it.

## Taken at `/plan`

1. **Tables by header.** A rules file's preamble holds tables told apart by their header row:
   `| target | anchor |`, `| setting | values | default | set by |`, and in the local file
   `| setting | value |`. A row under no known header is prose and not read.
2. **The declaration.** `setting` and each of `values` are code spans; `values` are separated by
   ` · `; `default` is one of them; `set by` is a rung's name as the entry file's ladders write
   it, or `the person`. A setting declared in two files is a diagnostic of the check and a
   refusal of the run.
3. **The condition.** `- **when** <setting>=<value>` beside `target` and `authority`, any number,
   all must hold; the setting must be declared and the value among its values, or the rule is
   refused as a malformed rule is — every mechanism in a tree is installed, so an undeclared
   setting is never a transient state.
4. **The value.** The local file's `| setting | value |` table; a setting absent stands at its
   default; a value no declaration holds is refused.
5. **Rendering.** A target's block holds the rules naming it whose conditions hold, in file order.
   A target named in the anchor table and left with no rule has no block: present, it is removed

# A tree carries only the method's text its settings call for — implementation plan

- **record of** what it intends to become

**Authored:** 2026-10-23

Implements [01-0010.0220](../tickets/01-0010.0220-a-tree-carries-the-methods-text-its-settings-call-for.md):
a mechanism declares its settings, a rule names the condition of its installation, the project
sets values in its local file, and the installer writes a rule into its targets only while its
condition holds. The decisions are
[q-0037.0006.0026](../questions/q-0037.0006.0026-how-does-a-project-choose-which-of-the-methods-text-its-tree-carries.md)'s,
its forms under *Proposed forms* and the passes after.

## Governing boundaries

- **The rules file's grammar** is the format shelf's
  ([MECHANISM-FORMAT.md](../../.agents/skills/mechanism/MECHANISM-FORMAT.md), *The rules file*):
  the anchor table, one section per rule, `target`, `authority`, `overrides`, the body between
  `<rule>` edges. The declaration table, the `when` line and the local file's settings table land
  there, as grammar; nothing here invents a second home.
- **The installer's contract** is the architecture's
  ([Installed blocks](../architecture.md#installed-blocks)): a named mode or a refusal; every
  target validated before anything is written; retraction byte-identical; a differing block
  refused until the caller says overwrite, then replaced whole and reported. A conditioned rule
  is one more thing the renderer reads; the contract does not move.
- **R7**: the project's answers live in `local.rules.md` and reach a file only as the local block.
  The settings table is one more thing that file authors; its values reach a file only through
  the installer.
- **R4**: an index is rendered on request and never committed beside its records. The
  consolidated settings table is an index of the declarations and the local file.
- **The entry file's *Autonomy***: the project sets each dial in its local block, and the agent
  never writes its dial — the host refuses the edit (01-0010.0125's shape).
- **The hosts edge** ([hosts.md](../edge/hosts.md)): the hook never fails the host; a problem
  becomes a line of context.
- **A document informs**: the edge record names the renderer; nothing reads the record to work.
- **Decision 2 of q-0037.0009.0021**: debugging's text reaches a tree as installed blocks of its
  own mechanism, never one text read behind a switch. This ticket supplies the switch; the
  mechanism is 01-0016.0020's.

## Impact

**Impact.** `inject_rules.py`: the parser reads tables by their header, reads a declaration table
and `when` lines, resolves settings from the local file's table or the default, renders a target's
block from the rules whose conditions hold, treats a target left with no rule as one whose block
is removed, and gains a run over every source and a call that changes a setting. Its check: a
`when` naming an undeclared setting or value, a local value no declaration holds, a setting
declared twice, a block whose content disagrees with the settings. `harness.py`'s `_install_rules`
is that run, so the install and the update read settings for free. The format shelf: three
forms. `local.rules.md` of this tree: a settings table. `/harness`: two occasions in its
description, the table shown. `/maintain`: the injector's check already reaches it as an
installed rule; a block disagreeing with its settings is one more diagnostic there, no new rule.
The hosts edge: a line at session start. Tests: `test_inject_rules.py` for every new form and
refusal, `test_harness.py` for the run.

**Hidden edges.** The anchor-table parser matches any row of two code spans, so a local settings
table of two code spans would be read as anchors: tables must be told by their header before
the first new row is written. A recipient updated before its local file has a table stands at
every default — safe, and the update's report says it. The dial's rows in the table are the
person's: the host's refusal of a dial edit must learn the table's row, or the table waits for
01-0010.0125. A run of the installer moves the entry file under running sessions
(01-0018.0010). Every mechanism's fingerprint moves at the format change. A setting's declaring
mechanism must exist before any rule can use it: `debug` has none until 01-0016.0020 builds
debugging, and the dials have none until the ladder mechanisms exist — the ticket's live
criteria have no declared setting to stand on (challenge 1).

**Leave alone.** The debug blocks' content and their move (01-0016.0020). Which method
(01-0017.0020). The host's refusal itself (01-0010.0125). The session-row writes of the hook.

**Recommendation.** Proceed as one slice, once the three challenges below are aligned: the
machinery is one contract; what is unsettled is which live setting proves it, where the wake's
line comes from, and what the edge record is.

## Challenges for `/align`

1. **No declared setting exists for the live criteria.** A `when` needs a declaring mechanism.
   `debug` is debugging's, unbuilt (01-0016.0020, *own align precedes*); the dials are the ladder
   mechanisms', undeclared (q-0037.0010.0002.0005, q-0037.0012.0001). The machinery can be proved
   whole on fixture trees — the suite already builds scratch repositories with rules files — but
   criteria 3 and 4 name this tree. Options: (a) the debugging mechanism's rules file lands with
   this ticket, holding the `debug` declaration, and the rules now reading *Under debug=on* in
   other mechanisms' files gain `when debug=on` — 01-0016.0020 shrinks to the texts that leave
   the entry file and the scripts; (b) criterion 3, the dial from the table, is deferred to the
   ladder mechanisms as a straw dog, the live proof being `debug` under (a); (c) the live
   criteria wait and the ticket proves itself on fixtures alone. Recommended: (a) with (b) —
   `debug` is the switch the whole question began with, and the dial has no declarer to wait for.
2. **The wake's line.** The decided flow has the wake report a tree whose blocks disagree with its
   settings. The wake is the questions mechanism's (`questions.py --hook` through `hook.sh`); the
   detector is the injector's check. Options: (a) `hook.sh` runs the injector's check after the
   wake and appends its one line in the host's form — `hook.sh` becomes a shared part, claimed
   by the always-on mechanism as every shared part is; (b) the questions mechanism calls the
   injector's check inside the wake — one mechanism's script reading another's, a *Relies on*
   row; (c) a second hook entry per host, owned by mechanism-shape and merged by the harness as
   core's hooks are — one more process at start, and the host-form code twice. Recommended: (a).

   edge record `docs/edge/settings.md`*. R4 forbids committing an index beside its records, and
   the edge format says a record informs and nothing reads it to work. Options: (a) the record is
   hand-written in the edge format — the contract, the invariants with their validators, and a

   never committed; (b) the decision stands and R4 takes an exception. Recommended: (a), the
   question's decision amended to it.

   `| target | anchor |`, `| setting | values | default | set by |`, and in the local file

   setting is never a transient state.

   default; a value no declaration holds is refused.

   A target named in the anchor table and left with no rule has no block: present, it is removed
   by retraction's cut and reported, as a dropped target is.
6. **The run.** `inject_rules.py --install --overwrite` with no slug installs every source in the
   harness's order — mechanisms, then local — and is `_install_rules`; the report carries each
   block replaced. Overwrite is said because a settings change makes a block differ from its

   existing *drifted* state already names.
10. **The dial line.** Deferred to challenge 1; until then L2 stands as it is.

## Shapes

- `Rule` gains `when`, the conditions as pairs; `RulesFile` gains its declarations; a resolution
  of settings — declarations across every rules file, values from the local file — is read once
  per run and passed to `block(target, settings)`. The parser's table reading is one function

- `_installing_or_retracting` plans a removal for a target whose rendering is empty, through
  `_removal`.
- `check` gathers declarations across files before judging any file.
- `harness.py` passes settings through `_install_rules`; the rehearsal reads the local file's

   header-keyed reader; the anchor tests unchanged.
2. **Declarations and conditions parsed** — red for each refusal of decisions 2 and 3; green.

4. **The run and the call** — red: `--install` with no slug refused; `--set` on an undeclared

5. **The check and the table** — the new diagnostics, the rendered table, `--settings` writing

6. **The format shelf and the skills** — the three forms on the shelf; `/harness`'s description
   and body; the hosts edge's line — after challenge 2.
7. **The live setting** — after challenge 1.

Every stage keeps the suite green; stage 1 changes no behaviour of a tree without a settings
table.

- Criterion 2 — stage 2's refusals and stage 5's diagnostics.
- Criterion 3 — challenge 1.

- Criterion 5 — challenge 3: as written it contradicts R4.

**Что мешает.** В дереве уже есть правило R4: такие сводные файлы не коммитят. Файл, который просто собирает в одном месте то, что другие файлы уже говорят о себе — тут объявления в файлах правил и значения в локальном файле, — называется индексом, и индекс рисуют по запросу, а в репозиторий не кладут. def _hook_specific(event: str, context: str, tag: str) -> str:
    return json.dumps({"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": event, "additionalContext": context}})


def _cursor_answer(event: str, context: str, tag: str) -> str:
    """Cursor drops a start hook's context (a confirmed host defect), and passes its `env` to
    every later hook of the session, so the session's tag goes there too, for whatever the agent's
    shell can read of it. Its prompt hook can only allow or block, and always allows: nothing here
    may hold back the person's message."""

def write(self, name: str, text: str) -> Path:
        """Place a record at a root-relative name, byte-exact — no newline translation."""
        path = self.root / name
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as handle:
            handle.write(text)
        return path

        f"- **target** `{TARGET}`\n"
        "- **authority** the user, 2026-10-23\n\n"
        "<rule>\nAlways here.\n</rule>\n\n"
        "## D2 — while debugging\n\n"
        f"- **target** `{TARGET}`\n"
        f"{when}"
        "- **authority** the user, 2026-10-23\n\n"
        "<rule>\nOnly while debugging.\n</rule>\n"
    )


def values_table(value: str | None) -> str:

    )

# edge — holds what the system promises those who consume it and requires of those who extend it, one record per edge

- **instruction** `.agents/skills/edge/SKILL.md` — the act: establishing a record, attaching an extension and passing its checks, monitoring, validating, deriving
- **state** installed
- **record of** what must always hold

## How it works

An **edge** is where the system meets someone outside it: a consumer of what it promises, or an
extender attaching to it — a host and its integration, a recipient project with its own
mechanisms. Each edge has one record: what is promised and what is required there, the checks a
new extension passes, where each extension stands, the edge's concerns and its roadmap. An edge
things attach to keeps one sidecar per extension, holding where that extension's integration lives
and its result for every check. The shape is the format shelf beside the skill; the maintainer
script holds every live record and sidecar to it.

**The record informs; the integration is elsewhere.** A record lives in the instance half, under
`docs/edge/`, and nothing an integration needs to work is read from it: the integration is code and
configuration in its own home, core where it ships, and the record names it *(the user,
2026-10-10)*. So a record may describe core, and core never depends on it. A recipient keeps its
own edges; this tree's records do not ship. Text a recipient meets about an edge — the front page,
an install guide — is derived from the record.

**The checks are the record's, the act is the skill's.** A record's `Extending` lists the checks
every extension passes, as a ticket lists its criteria; the skill's *Extend* goal is the
instruction to build an extension to the contract, pass those checks live, and write the sidecar.
Because every sidecar answers every check by name, a new extension is held to the same checks as
those before it, and a check added later shows at once as unanswered in every sidecar.

**A landed change writes its record in the same commit.** The occasion that most changes an edge
is a landing — a promise, a validator or a check, changed by delivered work — and a
live observation is made in the same work. Both reach `/verify` as an installed rule, E4, since
holding landed work to what governs it is where the occasion is read; without it the record would
be written only at alignment and in maintenance, and fall behind every landing *(the user,
2026-10-10)*.

**Maintenance fits `/maintain`'s model.** A record is of the code and configuration it names, so
when a pass's scope moves a named part the record is re-read against it, and a broken promise is
reported as drift. That duty reaches `/maintain` as an installed block, beside the check that
holds the form. Re-observing is live work and never a maintenance pass's.

**An observation keeps its date, and nothing marks it stale** *(the user, 2026-10-10)*. Its date,
beside the history of the code it watched, already says what it is worth; marking results stale
when a named part moved would cost a judgment at every landing and lose real observations, and
only the next live check acts on age, which runs when an extension is deliberately re-checked.

It is **installed**. A tree without it keeps no edge records; the parts table below is what an
installer adds and an uninstaller removes.

**Who decided each rule.**

| rule | decided by |
|---|---|
| E1 — the records are checked by `edges.py` | the user, 2026-10-10, owed to `/maintain`'s M1 |
| E2 — a record is held to what it names | the user, 2026-10-10: the maintenance rule fits maintenance |
| no staleness marking: an observation keeps its date | the user, 2026-10-10 |
| E3 — a plan is challenged against the edges it touches | the align skill's own text, moved here 2026-10-10 |
| E4 — a landed change at an edge writes its record, a live observation its sidecar | the user, 2026-10-10 |
| an edge is met by consumers and extenders, plugin-like shapes included | the user, 2026-10-10 |
| the record in `docs/edge/`, informing and never depended on | the user, 2026-10-10 |
| the general checks in the record, each extension's specifics in a sidecar | the user, 2026-10-10 |
| `Contract`, `Invariants` with inline validators, `Concerns`, `Roadmap`, the three statuses | with the selected skills, 2026-09-05 |

## Moments

| moment | instructed by | kind, and why |
|---|---|---|
| establishing an edge's record, or populating it from docs, tests and code | `.agents/skills/edge/SKILL.md` | |
| writing a record or a sidecar to its shape | `.agents/skills/edge/EDGE-FORMAT.md` | |
| attaching an extension and passing the record's checks live | `.agents/skills/edge/SKILL.md` | |
| passing the checks again for an extension that changed upstream | `.agents/skills/edge/SKILL.md` | |
| noticing that an extension changed upstream, a host's new version | — | <straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0023">not yet</straw-dog> |
| checking a change against the edges it touches, when asked | `.agents/skills/edge/SKILL.md` | |
| writing a record when a change at its edge lands | `.agents/skills/verify/SKILL.md` | |
| writing a live observation of an extension into its sidecar | `.agents/skills/verify/SKILL.md` | |
| challenging a plan against an edge's record | `.agents/skills/align/SKILL.md` | |
| validating code, tests and derived text against a record | `.agents/skills/edge/SKILL.md` | |
| deriving text for a consumer or an extender | `.agents/skills/edge/SKILL.md` | |
| checking live records and sidecars against the shape | `.agents/scripts/gw/edges.py` | |
| re-reading a record when a file it names moved | `.agents/skills/maintain/SKILL.md` | |
| writing an installation-edge change's line as it is made | — | <straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0020.0002.0001">not yet</straw-dog> |
| installing this mechanism into a tree, with the rest of core | `.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py` | |
| removing this mechanism from a tree | — | <straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0013.0002">not yet</straw-dog> |

## Install adds, uninstall removes

| part | where |
|---|---|
| instruction file | `.agents/skills/edge/SKILL.md` |
| format shelf | `.agents/skills/edge/EDGE-FORMAT.md` |
| this doc | `.agents/mechanisms/edge/edge.md` |
| its rules file | `.agents/mechanisms/edge/edge.rules.md` |
| the maintainer | `.agents/scripts/gw/edges.py` |
| the maintainer's tests | `.agents/scripts/gw/test/test_edges.py` |

## Relies on, and does not own

| part | where | owner |
|---|---|---|
| test harness | `.agents/scripts/gw/test/repository.py` | `mechanism-shape` |
| the installer | `.agents/scripts/gw/inject_rules.py` | `mechanism-shape` |
| the pass that re-reads a record | `.agents/skills/maintain/SKILL.md` | `maintain` |
| the status vocabulary a record's aggregation sections keep out | `.agents/skills/ticket/TICKET-FORMAT.md` | `ticket` |
| the challenge's heading in `/align`, where E3 is installed | `.agents/skills/align/SKILL.md` → "### Challenge against the Edge records" | `/align`'s own, its mechanism not yet |
| the installed rules' heading in `/verify`, where E4 is installed | `.agents/skills/verify/SKILL.md` → "## Installed from other mechanisms" | `/verify`'s own, its mechanism not yet |
| the method's vocabulary | `.agents/glossary.md` | nobody removable |

## What it produces, and who reads it

- **The edge records** — *what must always hold* — read by whoever plans or builds at an edge,
  through the challenge installed in `/align`; by the skill's *Extend* goal for the checks a new
  extension passes; by `/verify` under E4 when a change at the edge lands; by `/maintain` when a
  file a record names moves; and as the source of every
  text derived for a consumer or an extender.
- **The sidecars** — *what exists* — read by whoever attaches or re-checks that extension, by
  `/verify` under E4, and by `/maintain` under E2; each result is an observation as of its date, never a promise.
- **The maintainer's report** — *what exists* — read by `/verify` through the verification set and
  by `/maintain` under E1. Its exit status is what the set consumes; its JSON is for the person
  reading a failure. It writes nothing.
- **The rules file** — *what must always hold* — read by the installer alone, and by whoever amends
  a rule of this mechanism that another skill reads. Its blocks sit in `/maintain`, `/align` and
  `/verify`.

Nothing else; no index. The records directory is its own register.

## Not yet at the shape

**Two `not yet` rows of its own**, each bound to an open question: noticing a host's new version,
and the installation edge's line written as a change is made.

## What retires this

The system having no edge: nothing consumes it from outside and nothing attaches to it. A harness
installed into other projects across several hosts has both, so the condition does not arrive
while the harness is shared.

## What would show it working, graded by someone who did not build it

Pre-registered 2026-10-10, two graders.

**The session that next attaches an extension at an edge that already has some** grades the
record: did the record and the skill's *Extend* goal suffice to integrate and check it, without
reading the history the record was seeded from? Each time it had to go back to that history, or to
the code, for something the record should have said is a miss, named in the evidence.

**The session that writes the installation edge's record** grades the format: did a promised edge,
with no extensions and a different reader, fit the shape unchanged, or did the format have to be
rewritten to receive it? A format bent only for hosts would show here.

## The doc

```md
# <slug> — <what it is, in one line>

- **instruction** `<path>` — what it holds
- **state** always on
- **record of** what must always hold

## How it works

## Moments

## Install adds, uninstall removes

## Relies on, and does not own

## What it produces, and who reads it

## Not yet at the shape

## What retires this

## What would show it working, graded by someone who did not build it
```

Sections appear in this order. All but the two tables are prose and are never parsed — but two
absences are diagnostics. A doc missing the **grading** section names no grader, and has been
labelled rather than declared. A doc missing **What it produces, and who reads it** leaves its
outputs unaccounted: every artifact a mechanism emits or ships names its reader there — a person
at a stated moment, another mechanism, a script — or the section says why nobody reads it. Who the
reader is, and whether they are enough, is judgment and never the check's; that the question was
answered at all is not.

**An output listed by a bullet names its kind**, after its name, before its reader:
`- **<output>** — *<kind>* — <who reads it>`. The kind is one of the four kinds of record —
*what it intends to become*, *what must always hold*, *what exists*, *what happened* — or
*its format's*, for an output that is a record of another mechanism and takes the kind that
format declares. A record whose kind moves with its state names the first and the rule after
it: *what it intends to become, what happened once closed*. A bullet with no kind, or another,
is a diagnostic; the section's prose and nested bullets name no output.

**The title line names the job, not the procedure.** What the mechanism is for and holds true,
never the steps its script runs — a declaration written beside its implementation takes the
script's verbs, and a reader then cannot tell what the mechanism would still own if the
implementation changed.

### Header bullets

- **instruction** — backticked repo-relative path to a skill the mechanism owns, one bullet per
  skill, each the act at one of its moments. Required, and never the doc itself.
- **state** — `always on` or `installed`, and nothing else. `always on` means nothing can install
  or uninstall it, so it has no lifecycle scripts and that absence is a property. It is what tells
  a reader which way to read the parts table.
- **record of** — `what must always hold`, and nothing else: the doc is the record its
  instruction is repaired to. This format is the kind's authored home; the bullet is the kind
  where an agent editing the doc meets it, and the check holds the two equal. The bullet's
  earlier name, `kind`, is reported.
- There is no evidence bullet. The evidence is a record declared under [Records](#the-evidence-is-a-record-of-the-shape)
  below and found by the slug; the doc never names it, since it is the instance's and a recipient
  does not have it. Which ticket declared the mechanism is the evidence's first paragraph *(the
  user, 2026-09-09)*: the one check that read such a bullet is replaced by the rule that a
  `not yet` row may not wait on a question already answered, which needs no field.

## Moments

```md
| moment | instructed by | kind, and why |
```

- **moment** — the occasion, in the words a person would use for it.
- **instructed by** — a backticked path, or `—`.
- **kind, and why** — empty when the row is instructed. Otherwise one of `elsewhere`,
  `embedded`, `unowned by design`, `not yet`, a clause saying why, and — for all but
  `unowned by design` — its referent.

A row carries an instruction or an absence, never both and never neither.

A `not yet` row is a straw dog *(the user, 2026-09-20)*:

```md
| ordering the queue | — | <straw-dog question="q-N">not yet</straw-dog> |
```

Body: the kind alone; the referent is the question, and its words are the reason. A row
waiting on a question that is due, merged or superseded is a diagnostic. Unwrapped is unbound.
The shear strips the wrapper, so no id of this tree ships. The lister reports the row; this
check rules on the gap.

## The two tables

```md
| part | where |                 under "Install adds, uninstall removes"
| part | where | owner |         under "Relies on, and does not own"
```

The first title is its definition: **if uninstalling would not remove it, it is not a
part**. For an `always on` mechanism the same table is what a person moving it between
trees takes.

Relied-on parts never become an owner column on the first table — they are not added
by install, so listing them there contradicts its title.

**part** is a role name and may repeat. **where** is a backticked repo-relative path,
optionally with an anchor:

```
`.agents/skills/align/SKILL.md` → "### Challenge against the Edge records"
```

The phrase after `→` is checked as a verbatim substring of the file named. An owned part
is a whole file: in another's file a mechanism owns only what it installs there, which
its rules file names. The anchor serves a relied-on line — a heading another skill
carries, where a block is installed — so a line moved or renamed fails the check.

## Records

A mechanism that writes records declares each one where that record's format is declared — a
format file beside its instruction file, or its skill where the format is small; never its doc.
Three fields:

- **what a record is** — one file, one directory, or one row of a file that holds many.
- **tier** — when it is read.
- **what removes an entry** — the condition; `kept by design` where nothing does; or `not yet`,
  a straw dog bound to the question it waits on.

A record declared without all three is a diagnostic, and so is a mechanism that writes records and
declares none.

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0004">
Neither diagnostic is emitted yet: finding a mechanism that owes a record declaration needs
`record-bearing` to be a declared field, which it is not. Until then the two sentences above are a
rule with no check behind them.
</straw-dog>

## Parsing

| part | where |
|---|---|
| instruction file | `.agents/skills/questions/SKILL.md` |
| this doc | `.agents/mechanisms/questions/questions.md` |
| the records' format | `.agents/skills/questions/QUESTION-FORMAT.md` |

Mechanism: harness

The source is always the repository, cloned fresh at a ref; a working tree is never read. Where
that repository is, this tree says once:

Repository: https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness.git

That is the only authored home of it. The script reads its default `--from` there, an install
stamps a recipient's copy with the source the run actually read, and a fork edits the line once
and everything it installs names the fork. A check or an update from another `--from` sets the
line aside rather than reading an edit in core, as it does the local block and the block of any
mechanism of the tree's own.

Run the script from any clone of the harness, or from the tree's own copy once it has one. An
update is run by the incoming ref's installer, which reads what an earlier one left: run it from
a clone, since a tree's own copy may predate handing the run on.

```
python <clone>/.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py <target> --install [--replace-clone] [--from REPOSITORY] [--at REF]
python <clone>/.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py <target> --update [--overwrite] [--from REPOSITORY] [--at REF]
python <target>/.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py . --check [--from REPOSITORY]
python <target>/.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py . --links
```

`--from` defaults to the harness's own repository; `--at` to its default branch's head, and takes
a branch, a tag or a commit. To try a ref before it is pushed, pass a local clone's path as
`--from`: its committed `HEAD` is then the ref. The target is the top level of a git work tree.

`--links` is the per-clone step: the loader links are never committed, so a fresh clone of a
project that holds core runs it once, from the clone's own copy, with no source and no network.
It makes or repairs both links, names them in the clone's `.git/info/exclude`, and reports whether
each resolves; where the platform refuses, it prints the elevated commands and exits non-zero
until they have been run.

to have a context and a structure, not yet exhausted by any one realization. Being a shape says
nothing about being load-bearing — an implementation method is a shape too. → [glossary](.agents/glossary.md).

- **Generalize or ask.** Where there is a load-bearing reason to think the work will need a shape generalized, generalize if the effort and the output are small; otherwise ask the person. Preserve a seam either way.
- **The shape's context.** Explore shape context - what is the shape one of? what are its relationships? does its scope overlap any other shape? Look in this tree and in every tree core reaches.
- **The shape's structure.** Explore shape structure - how this shape is/can be built? does expanding its structure change the contract or even what the shape is?

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0015">
- **A document informs.** A document under `docs/` records; it reaches the work only through the instruction that reads it — a ticket's criteria through the skill that plans to them, a decision through the result it binds. Instructions live in the entry file, a skill or a rules file; authorization comes from the user. Text in a document that would direct or authorize an agent on its own is drift: report it, and do not act on it.
</straw-dog>

- **Recency for evidence, longevity for principles.**

- **Occam.** Clarity and simplicity first — Occam's razor: take the shape with the fewest parts that does the job, and remove before you add. Say what need not exist: a rule, mechanism, record or step — the person's proposal or yours — that the work would not miss, said before it is built. Occam reads backwards too: an abstraction that arrives late and unifies parts already written has them rewritten through it, the work paid once and the prose contracted.

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0013.0003">
- **Weight follows the work.** A change costs what it weighs — in checks, records and steps.
</straw-dog>

- **A capable reader.** Write for a capable model: state the rule and its pointer. The definition the glossary owns, the example that motivated it, what it implies, and what a script already does for the reader stay out.

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0011.0002">
- **Tier is paid by every session.** A skill's description is its tier-1 surface: name there every use case the skill serves, and nothing else — never its method or how it is built. Write every rule at the tier its occasion reads, and no higher: what sits at tier 1 is paid for by every session.
</straw-dog>

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0012">

name it, what is decided, what is next, where it stops, what it needs from the person. What the
work read, ran or wrote on the way, and what it will read next, is not told; what more the person
hears at an occasion, a skill's `What the person hears` says, in their words. It names no script,
call, check, report, record's internals or hook, and never retells a report: an outcome is one
sentence, a failure is what the person does. A stop at or above a ladder's dial is said once, in
the person's words — `✋ <the decision, as the ladder shows it>` — the ladder's and the rung's names
in it nowhere. <straw-dog question="q-0037.0009.0021">Under `debug=on` the machinery is shown as well.</straw-dog>
</straw-dog>

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0009.0021">

judgement, is named at its authored home and cited by that name. Under `debug=on`, an item shown

## Document load-bearing, code&comment the rest

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">
A project's architecture, ADRs and glossary are the home for:
- Constitution — identity semantics, consistency model, source-of-truth rules
- Structure — service boundaries, data ownership, event/data flows, extension seams
- Load-bearing — see the definition below

A decision forms in the body of the question it answers and lands in one of these as it is made —
as a straw dog while an open question's answer can still change it. A decision about a
mechanism lands in that mechanism's doc, and what was refuted in its evidence.
</straw-dog>

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">
Bad architectural documentation:
- Forecasts are stored in MongoDB collection forecast_hourly.

Better:
- Historical forecast issues must remain independently addressable by (location, valid_time, issue_time) because validation compares what was known at different issue times.
</straw-dog>

## What makes a thing "load-bearing"

- A decision or invariant whose violation would cause multiple parts of the system to become wrong, not merely require local refactoring.
- A thing is load-bearing when several of these are true: has high blast radius, crosses boundaries (i.e. services, persistence, APIs, ownership), other decisions depend on it, it protects an invariant,
is expensive to reverse, holds non-obvious rationale, long-standing.

- Counter-test: if it can be changed locally without understanding the rest of the architecture, it is not load-bearing.

## The loop

Two rings, joined at /align.

    session:   wake with /recall → /align → /conclude → (next session)
    delivery:  /ticket → /plan → /implement → /verify → /maintain → /ticket

/align opens the delivery ring and is where it returns whenever a decision is needed:
<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">a load-bearing shape is aligned on its question until its `Where it stands` is accepted,</straw-dog> /plan when the governing docs contradict, /verify when a finding needs one, /maintain when maintenance surfaces one. /ticket⇄/plan and /implement⇄/verify iterate as pairs.

Human checkpoints: every decision at /align; a question's `Where it stands` accepted; and
whatever stands at or above its ladder's dial under [Autonomy](#autonomy).

Do not reopen an accepted decision without new evidence.

### Helpers

- /impact determines the scope and load-bearingness of the shape. Use it to evaluate work volume and its ticketing shape (<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">an align on its question for load-bearing work, tickets for mechanical</straw-dog>), work units slicing or whether a shape deserves further investigation due to hidden complexity.
- /discover to investigate hidden complexity, by detecting what else the shape is.

## Self-improvement

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0012">
- A rule that was in place and did not fire was usually worded wrong. Register the failure in docs/rule-failures.md, or strike the entry it repeats, and propose the amendment that would have made it fire; /mechanism and /skill-up hold the means. Land the amendment in the same pass, showing its text first.
- A slip no rule covers is registered there too, described broadly enough to recognise its repeat;
  one proposes no rule.
- Keeping the register: an entry names the rules that were in play and proposes the amendment; a repeat strikes the entry it repeats rather than opening a second; an entry closes when its amendment lands, or is refused with its reason. Nothing here authorises deleting a rule.
</straw-dog>

## Autonomy

Autonomy is a dial on a ladder. A method whose decisions differ in how far their consequences
reach has a ladder, its rungs ordered by that reach and declared by the method's mechanism; a
method without one states which of its decisions are the agent's and which the person's. A
decision's rung is read from what it decides, never from the record that holds it; a case between
two rungs takes the higher.

- 🤖 Below the dial the agent settles and acts on its own.
- ✋ At the dial it settles, and shows the person before acting.
- 💬 Above it, it settles nothing: it brings the options and a recommendation, and the person
  decides.

A question carries its highest rung on each ladder it touches and stops for the person while that
rung is at or above the ladder's dial. Mending a violation is the work of the rung the mended thing
is on. Work closes with its commit once `/verify` passes on it; a push follows the project's way of
working with git, as its local file states.

The project sets each dial in its local block; an unset dial is at the lowest rung. The agent never
writes its dial<straw-dog question="q-0037.0006.0005">, and the host refuses an edit that changes it</straw-dog>.

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0010.0002.0005">
Development's ladder, lowest first:

| rung | a decision on it — as the person is shown it |
|---|---|
| code | writing the code inside agreed work |
| a feature | what one piece of work should deliver |
| load-bearing | a load-bearing architectural decision, e.g. module boundaries |
| a product slice | what gets built next |
| the whole product | what the project is for |

An install proposes the dial at *a feature*.
</straw-dog>

<straw-dog question="q-0037.0012.0001">
Self-improvement's ladder, lowest first:

| rung | a decision on it — as the person is shown it |
|---|---|
| a wording | rewording an instruction, its meaning unchanged |
| a script | fixing a script that carries an instruction out |
| a rule | changing an instruction or a skill |
| the method | changing the way of working |

An install proposes the dial at *a rule*.
</straw-dog>

## Straw dogs

Wrap anything an open question's answer will change, as you write it — or, for text already
written, in the pass that opens the question: `<straw-dog question="q-N">`, bound to the question
whose answer will rewrite it, or in code a `TODO` naming `q-N` first. Treat *not yet*, *until*,
*once it exists*, *for now*, *untested* in your own text as the same signal: find the question, or
open one. Wrap at the authored home, never where the harness installs or derives it. Write the body
to stand on its own: it is what a recipient receives once the wrapper is stripped, so it names no
question or ticket — the binding does. Leave what no open question would change unwrapped.

Follow a straw dog like any other rule until it is due, as the listing and the wake report; then
act on reality, rewrite it to what is now true, and do not treat the contradiction as a violation.

## 63. A hand-edited setting was received on wake, and two thirds of its rule stayed in a skill nobody opened 

**Rules in play:** [`/harness`](../.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md), *A tree whose local file was
edited by hand*, tier 2: *"run `inject_rules.py --install` before the first reply, at the rung of
the setting that changed, and say in one line what the tree now carries. The entry file has then
moved under the session: read it again before replying"*; the installer's wake line, tier 1 at
that occasion, as [the settings edge](edge/settings.md) states it: *told so at a session's start*;
[the hosts edge](edge/hosts.md), *Wake*.

**What happened.** The person set `debug` to `off` by hand in the local file's settings table,
then opened a fresh chat, to see whether the next session brings the tree to match — criterion 6 of
[01-0010.0220](tickets/01-0010.0220-a-tree-carries-the-methods-text-its-settings-call-for.md).
The wake carried the installer's line: two things out of step, run the installer, then the check.
The session ran both before its first reply and the check came back clean. Then the reply opened
with the entry-contract line the install had just taken out of the entry file, and said what the
tree now carried as a paragraph inside the recall, not as one line.

**Why it did not fire.** The rule's home is `/harness`, a skill a session opens when asked about
the harness or to change a setting. The occasion is a wake, where no skill is open and nothing
sends the session to that one. What reached the session was the wake line, and the line carries
one of the rule's three steps — the install — and neither the re-read nor the one-line report.
The install fired because the line said it; the rest did not because nothing at the occasion did.
The rule is worded for a reader who has it in front of them, and at its occasion nobody does.
